title: The Missing Mass: A Critical Appraisal of Thermodynamic, Stoichiometric, and Methodological Claims in a Recent Body Recomposition Review
content: A recent structured review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition sets out to synthesize the literature on body recomposition. In one of its early passages, it explains why higher-adiposity individuals can build muscle in a caloric deficit: their bodies "essentially have an energy surplus internally (stored fat) even when in an external caloric deficit." The sentence is intended as a heuristic. It is, in fact, internally inconsistent: a caloric deficit is defined by the depletion of endogenous energy stores, and if adipose tissue is being depleted, the body is not in an energy surplus – internal or otherwise. What the passage describes is a compartmental flux: stored lipid is oxidized to supply ATP for anabolic processes while total body energy declines. The distinction matters, because it is the difference between a model that specifies which tissue is changing and through what mass fluxes, and a model that does not. The present analysis examines whether this ambiguity recurs throughout the review. Five classes of issue are considered: (i) the treatment of thermal energy (kcal) without accompanying mass fluxes or excretory stoichiometry; (ii) the omission of whole-body nitrogen balance and the conflation of energy balance with energy availability; (iii) the operationalization of fat-free mass as skeletal muscle without glycogen/water correction or method-specific least-significant-change thresholds; (iv) unparameterized computational simulations presented as evidence, alongside internally inconsistent PRISMA counts and arithmetic contradictions – including a weight-loss target of −0.5–7.0% body mass·wk⁻¹ and an inverted deficit-to-fat-loss relationship in the 12-week plan; and (v) at least nine citation mismatches. A minimal corrective framework is proposed – compartmental mass balance, explicit nitrogen accounting, method-specific measurement thresholds, transparent computational provenance, and reconciled reporting – as a set of requirements that would strengthen any synthesis in this field. The analysis builds on earlier observations of similar conceptual issues in related ISSN documents.
